sources.title: NGSS MS-LS1-3: Use argument supported by evidence for how the body is a system of interacting subsystems composed of groups of cells
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.1 Organs and Structures of the Respiratory System
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.3 The Process of Breathing

note.text: Air from your nose and mouth goes down the trachea, or windpipe.
Rings of cartilage hold the trachea open, so it never collapses.

steps.title: Bronchi
steps.instruction: Trace the branching tubes into each lung.

note.text: The trachea splits into two bronchi, which branch again and again into tiny tubes, like an upside-down tree.
note.remember: Air path: trachea, bronchi, air sacs.

note.text: The lungs are spongy organs filled with the branching tubes and millions of tiny air sacs.

steps.title: Diaphragm
steps.instruction: Trace the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs.

note.text: When the diaphragm contracts, it moves down, making more space. The lungs stretch and air rushes in.

steps.title: Air sacs
steps.instruction: Trace the cluster of tiny air sacs, shown enlarged.

note.text: Each air sac, or alveolus, is only about 0.2 mm across. This is where gases are exchanged.

steps.title: Capillary
steps.instruction: Draw the blood capillary next to the air sacs.

note.text: Oxygen diffuses from the air sacs into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses out to be breathed away.
note.remember: Air sacs: oxygen in, CO2 out.

steps.title: Name the parts
steps.instruction: Pick the name for each numbered part.

targets.role: Carries air down to the lungs.

mistakes.Esophagus: The esophagus carries food. This ringed tube carries air: the trachea.

steps.title: Breathing in
steps.question: What happens when you breathe in?

options.text: The diaphragm contracts and moves down, so the chest gets bigger and air flows in
options.feedback: Yes. Muscles between the ribs help too, lifting the rib cage outward.

options.text: The lungs suck air in on their own
options.feedback: Lungs have no muscle to do that. The diaphragm and rib muscles make the space.
When it contracts it moves down, making more room for the lungs.
The heart pumps blood. Breathing is powered by the diaphragm.

steps.title: Teamwork
steps.question: Why do the air sacs need to be wrapped in blood capillaries?

options.text: So oxygen can pass straight into the blood and travel to every cell
options.feedback: Right. The respiratory system brings oxygen in; the circulatory system carries it to the body.

options.text: To keep the air sacs warm
options.feedback: The capillaries are there for gas exchange: oxygen into the blood, CO2 out.
Capillaries carry blood. They pick up oxygen from the air sacs.
Without capillaries, oxygen in the lungs couldn't reach the body's cells.
